report:
Based on high-quality recent clinical evidence, taking probiotics does **not** reliably shorten the duration of acute infectious diarrhea.

While early meta-analyses suggested probiotics might reduce illness duration by about 24 hours, rigorous updated research indicates otherwise:

* **Updated Cochrane Review (2020):** Evaluating trials with low risk of bias, Cochrane concluded that probiotics likely make little to no difference in diarrhea duration or the likelihood of diarrhea lasting 48 hours or longer [Cochrane Review](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea).
* **Large Clinical Trials (2018):** Two multicenter, randomized controlled trials published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* evaluated widely used probiotic formulations (*Lactobacillus rhamnosus* GG and a *L. rhamnosus* / *L. helveticus* combination) in children with acute gastroenteritis. Neither trial demonstrated a reduction in symptom duration or disease severity compared to placebo [Freedman et al.](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802597), [Schnadower et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30462938/).
* **Medical Guidelines:** The American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) recommends against the routine use of probiotics for acute infectious gastroenteritis, citing a lack of proven clinical benefit [AGA Guidelines](https://www.gastrojournal.org/article/S0016-5085(20)34729-6/fulltext).

**Conclusion:** Probiotics do not meaningfully shorten the duration of acute infectious diarrhea. Fluid rehydration and supportive care remain the standard and primary treatments.
